overview: Ur was a city in southern Mesopotamia, in today’s Iraq, and sometimes the capital of a much larger kingdom. Its long history includes early settlements, royal dynasties and later life under other rulers. The map’s 4000 to 1500 BCE span and enormous repeated outline are not the lifetime or reliable borders of one Ur kingdom. They must not be read as continuous control over the whole shaded region.

periods.title: Early settlement and city rulers
periods.summary: Ur grew into an important third-millennium city with Gulf trading connections and royal tombs.

periods.title: The Third Dynasty of Ur
periods.summary: This imperial phase, conventionally about 2112 to 2004 BCE, was much shorter than the map record.

periods.title: The city under successor kingdoms
periods.summary: Isin, Larsa and Babylon competed for the south. Ur’s households and schools continued after its dynasty fell.

sections.title: A river city and an imperial capital

items.text: Ur grew beside the Euphrates, with waterways connecting it to the Persian Gulf. By the third millennium BCE it was a major urban center, able to obtain materials from far beyond southern Mesopotamia. Its patron deity was Nanna, the moon god. Trade, farming and the institutions of worship all helped shape this river city.

Around 2100 BCE, Ur-Nammu brought southern Mesopotamian cities under his rule and sponsored temples, including the ziggurat at Ur. A ziggurat was a monumental stepped platform associated with a temple. Its upper levels have not survived: modern drawings reconstruct them from evidence and comparison, while the visible lower stages have also undergone restoration.

Beneath the walls of Ur’s temple of Nimintabba, excavators found sealed brick boxes containing stone tablets and copper figures carrying baskets on their heads. Their inscriptions name King Shulgi and commemorate the temple’s construction. These foundation deposits joined engineering with ritual: important words and images were deliberately placed where later worshippers would not normally see them.

An inscription of Ur-Namma claims that he drained a marsh planted with young date palms and built a levee, dedicating the reclaimed area to Ur. He even gave the levee a name meaning “Who is like Nanna?” This is a king advertising his work, but it shows how water management and productive land featured in royal ideas of achievement.

The famous Royal Cemetery was not made up entirely of spectacular royal tombs. Excavators uncovered about 1,850 burials, most of them simple graves. The exceptional gold vessels and imported stones show what a small, wealthy group could command. Southern Mesopotamia had no local gold deposits, so those glittering objects also point outward to networks of exchange.

The object called the Standard of Ur, made around 2550 to 2400 BCE, combines shell, red limestone and blue lapis lazuli in mosaics. One scene shows a banquet with a singer and lyre player; another depicts warfare and captives. Its original purpose remains uncertain. The surviving decoration offers a royal view of power and celebration, rather than a picture of every family’s dinner.

A seal from Puabi’s tomb gives a short writing sample: “pu₃-ad / nin.” This is a scholarly Roman-letter transliteration of cuneiform, not the original wedge shapes. The Cuneiform Digital Library translates it “Pu-abum, the queen”; museums commonly call her Puabi. The mid-third-millennium lapis seal, now British Museum 121544, connects a named woman with royal status and a richly furnished burial.

The early second-millennium house that excavators named No. 3 Straight Street had an L-shaped entrance leading into a paved courtyard. A drain occupied the center, while low brick stands may have supported water jars. This address is an archaeologist’s label, not a surviving ancient street sign. The layout lets us trace movement from the street into household space.

In the same house, a small paved room beneath the staircase had a drain. Leonard Woolley interpreted it as a lavatory. Another little drained room beside the reception area was interpreted as a washing place. These are specific archaeological interpretations of rooms and plumbing traces, giving us a rare glimpse of the less glamorous business of keeping a house usable.

The kitchen at No. 3 Straight Street contained a circular bread oven, a raised brick cooking hearth and an open fireplace. The equipment occupied a different room from the central courtyard and reception area. Ancient dinner left an architectural footprint: even when food and wooden utensils disappeared, ovens and hearths remained for excavators to find.

sections.title: Lessons, trade and a rattling pig

items.text: More than two thousand texts came from No. 7 Quiet Street, a house identified as a place of scribal teaching. They include accounts, word lists, mathematics and literature; dateable examples belong to the first half of the eighteenth century BCE. Two copies of the same composition differ in spelling, which scholar Steve Tinney suggests could record two students taking dictation together.

Around 1750 BCE, a customer named Nanni complained to the merchant Ea-nasir about poor-quality copper delivered after a Gulf voyage, as well as trouble and delay with another delivery. The clay letter was excavated at Ur. Long-distance trade created opportunities, but also arguments about what had been promised. This particular unhappy customer’s complaint proved remarkably durable.

A clay pig from Ur has a hollow body with little clay balls inside: shake it and it rattles. Animal rattles became especially common in the early second millennium BCE. British Museum researcher Enrica Inversi argues that such objects could be toys as well as musical or protective objects. A pig could make a useful noise without needing to be fed.

New excavations in 2015 returned to Ur’s old Niche Lane area and found balance-pan weights and economic texts, supporting earlier evidence for merchants there. Small objects like these can reveal ordinary work as clearly as a gold treasure reveals wealth. The renewed excavations also showed why older bricks reused in a house cannot by themselves date the whole building.

sections.title: Changes of ruler and a much longer city life

items.text: The Third Dynasty of Ur collapsed around 2004 BCE. Rulers of Isin took control of Ur and Nippur, and subsequent struggles brought Larsa and Babylon to prominence in the south. A city could lose its position as an imperial capital while still supporting homes, traders and scribal learning. The later household evidence on this card belongs to that changed political world.

Long after the map stops, the sixth-century BCE Babylonian king Nabonidus repaired Ur’s ziggurat. His inscription says he read earlier records naming Ur-Namma and Shulgi, then restored the damaged structure with bitumen and baked bricks. Clay cylinders preserve his account. Ur’s buildings already had a deep past that later rulers investigated and claimed a place within.

ending.text: Ur’s imperial dynasty fell around 2004 BCE amid an Elamite attack; Isin and other kingdoms followed. The city continued long beyond the map’s 1500 BCE cutoff. Archaeologist W. B. Hafford links eventual abandonment to the Euphrates shifting away. Loss of independence, later urban decline and the survival of written traditions were different processes.
